content: INFS4205/7205 Personalised Multimodal Agent System. 1. Introduction General chatbots are good at giving the most basic flow of reply, but they cannot maintain user interests over time, conversational preferences, or situational awareness across interactions. As users tend to move across various topics naturally and still expect that their responses can be contextually relevant and adaptive, this approach has come alive in real conversations. Recent studies have revealed evidence that retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) may enhance factual grounding and reduce hallucination for LLM systems (Lewis et al., 2020). This project has an aim to make use of multimodal retrieval in conversational memory combined with lightweight agent orchestration to enhance personalised conversational retrieval in more comprehensive and realistic user-centred interactions. In order to validate this idea, we build a lightweight LangGraph-based agent that performs memory-aware query rewriting, multimodal retrieval selection, query routing, and grounded response generation for different query families. 2. Knowledge Base Construction Building the knowledge base The knowledge base was predominantly built on topics that surfaced from normal conversations with ChatGPT, and consequently the dataset became large and intuitive. Rather than focusing on one narrow domain, the data you collected included EventNow project materials and UI screenshots, travel and cultural visuals related to Japan and New Zealand, K-pop and fashion-related images, game-related content, handwritten study notes, and some general wellbeing and lifestyle discussions. Moreover, the system was personalised as the dataset was representative of the user’s individual interests, interaction behaviors, and conversational style. The aim was not to create a focused benchmark chatbot, but rather to generate a more realistic chat assistant that could move back and forth between various topics, remember your preferences and facilitate more natural follow-up conversations. Text documents were first segmented into smaller semantic chunks for semantic similarity analysis. Text content was represented with manually written image captions, true image embeddings including metadata tags (modality type, document family, section category and visual type). Early retrieval experiments indicated that while the retrieval pipeline achieved adequate performance, retrieval quality was often poor due to the emergence of semantically similar but contextually irrelevant chunks. Problems involved overly general chunking, poor metadata coverage, and semantic similarities between conversational topics. To improve retrieval quality, several iterations were tested, including chunk size adjustment, metadata-based section filtering, query- family routing, hybrid retrieval, fallback retrieval and personalised retrieval strategies. The final system implemented retrieval based on embedding and thus supported conversational and multimodal semantic matching more efficiently than simple keyword search. Retrieval experiments compared text-only retrieval, image-only retrieval, hybrid retrieval and Agentic RAG workflows for different query families. content: The system is based on a LangGraph-based agent workflow to handle memory management, query routing, retrieval selection, and grounded response generation. Rather than employing a static RAG pipeline for each query, the agent responds to the type of query made and the conversation with the user by dynamically determining how it can and should address the query. Upon request from a user, the system checks conversational memory such as past interests, topics, dialogue patterns, etc., to begin with. Then in a memory conscious query rewrite phase I use to rewrite ambiguous follow-up questions with context of the last conversation. The router then classifies the query family — factual retrieval, cross-modal retrieval, analytical reasoning or personalised conversational queries. The planner is then tasked with choosing the best retrieval strategy. It supports multiple retrieval tools such as text retrieval, picture caption retrieval, true-image retrieval, hybrid retrieval, and personalised hybrid retrieval. These tools are fed with a multimodal knowledgebase that includes text chunks, image captions, true images, and metadata with attributes stored in a vector-base of information. The ret

The returned evidence is fed into the LLM generation step, generating grounded answers. A relatively lightweight verification step is also added to alleviate unsupported output and make retrieval more grounded. Lastly, this memory state is updated to reflect newly generated preference/conversational focus to cater later on to personalised interactions. An agent workflow was essential in the sense that the query families required different retrieval behaviours, reasoning paths. No single memory retrieval pipeline had the scope to support conversational memory, multimodal retrieval, or ambiguous follow up inquiries, therefore the LangGraph agent fulfills a lightweight controller role to orchestrate dynamic dynamics in the whole system. 5. Results and Analysis Figure 3 and Figure 4 present a memory ablation study. Without memory, vague follow-up queries were expanded using only generic visual keywords, leading to unrelated retrieval results. With memory enabled, the system preserved conversational context and expanded the query using previous user preferences, improving personalised retrieval behaviour. The experiments revealed that Hybrid RAG exhibited the best retrieval grounding whilst Agentic RAG outperformed in personalised and multi-hop queries. Agentic RAG performed best on personalised and multi-hop queries, while Hybrid RAG remained particularly effective for cross-modal retrieval tasks. This indicates that routing, memory, and tool orchestration become more useful as query complexity increases.

The results also exhibited multiple trade-offs: hybrid retrieval enhanced grounding quality but introduced latency and complexity, while Agentic RAG reduced latency through more selective routing and orchestration. The memory ablation also revealed that conversational state could lead to improved personalised retrieval but it could also lead to instability when context was ambiguous. Although the absolute LLM-as-Judge scores were modest, the evaluation was mainly used as a relative comparison between system variants. The lower score range reflects the limited size of the personalised knowledge base, the use of local lightweight models, and the strict grounding-focused judge prompt. 7. Failure Cases A number of restrictions were identified with respect to the implementation of the personalised multimodal agent. One significant problem was retrieval instability related to semantic overlaps within the highly personalised dataset. Because many conversational topics had similar visual or emotional semantics, search results from embedding-based retrieval could still misplace the context, even with high semantic similarity scores. For instance, vague aesthetic or “

content: r emotional semantics, search results from embedding-based retrieval could still misplace the context, even with high semantic similarity scores. For instance, vague aesthetic or “similar vibe” queries sometimes brought back content about BTS instead of an image of travel from Japan due to more visually dominant entertainment representations being semantically overrepresented through retrieval. A second limitation relates to conversational memory and preference persistence. Memory-aware query rewriting was able to help with follow-up interactions, but was prone to over-relying on the context of the conversation, while erring with respect to longer-term preferences. This sometimes caused preference drift during extended conversations, as retrieval tended to favour the most recent topic in the conversation instead of consistent user interests. The experiments indicated that conversational memory resulted in better personalised retrieval; however, it was destabilizing when conversational intent was not clear anymore. The LangGraph workflow had done work to facilitate dynamic retrieval across query families, but routing decisions revolved around basic similarity patterns, metadata coverage, and rule-based query interpretation. This meant subjective conversational queries could sometimes elicit incorrect retrieval tools or weak grounding behaviour. These failures highlighted the extent to which personalised multimodal systems are affected, not only by retrieval quality but also by memory consistency, semantic balance and orchestration dependability. Some future improvements would be re-ranking, more dense metadata labelling, stronger long-term memory management and LLM-based routing. 8. Conclusion The findings show that multimodal retrieval, conversational memory, and lightweight agent orchestration can enhance personalised conversational interactions over that of relying on a static retrieval pipeline. Across the experiments, Hybrid RAG provided the best overall retrieval grounding, whereas Agentic RAG grew increasingly useful for conversational follow-up and multi-hop personalised queries where memory and routin

content: provided the best overall retrieval grounding, whereas Agentic RAG grew increasingly useful for conversational follow-up and multi-hop personalised queries where memory and routing matters more. However, the project also demonstrated that tailored multimodal systems are also vulnerable to overlapping semantic ideas, conversational uncertainty, and unstable memory in general, especially with a large, tailored knowledge base. In sum, the project helped me realize that quality of retrieval isn't just about the LLM, it is also about how knowledge is represented, retrieved, filtered, and orchestrated with different conversational settings. What could be improved is more robust reranking, more faithful long-term memory mechanisms and adaptive routing for ambiguous conversational queries. Final agent: LangGraph + memory rewrite + router + selected retrieval tool + grounded generation.
